project.topic: What if light disappeared for 5 seconds?
project.title: What if light disappeared for 5 seconds?
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If every bit of light vanished for just five seconds, how long would it really take for everything to light up again?
project.viewer_takeaway: Light takes time to travel, so after a five-second blackout lamps return instantly, sunlight takes over eight minutes, and the stars stay dark for years: about 4.4 for the southern sky’s Alpha Centauri, 8.6 for Sirius, the first star most northern viewers would see.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second: from a lamp to your eye in nanoseconds, from the Sun in about 499 s, from the nearest star in over four years.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: For five seconds, every photon in the universe vanishes and no light can exist, including light already on its way. After that, everything shines normally again. Nothing else changes.
assumptions: Light in transit is erased, not paused.
Sources resume immediately after five seconds.
The street and the people are illustrative; the night sky uses real star positions for a city at 38 degrees south on a mid-February night.
Daylight, moonlight and planet light are all sunlight, so they return with it; no bright planet is in the parts of the sky the night shots look at.
causal_chain: All light vanishes for five seconds; you see eigengrau.
Nearby lamps and screens return within nanoseconds.
Sunlight is 150 million km away and needs about 8 minutes 19 seconds.
Until it arrives, noon is lit only by artificial light under a starless black sky.
Daylight floods back within about two seconds, 8 min 24 s after the dark began.
That night the Moon is back but no stars.
Starlight in transit was erased; after the Sun, the nearest naked-eye star (Alpha Centauri, southern sky) is 4.37 light-years away.
Alpha Centauri returns after about 4.4 years; from mid-northern latitudes the first star is Sirius, after 8.6; others over decades to millennia.
uncertainties: Exactly how the eye adapts in five seconds varies from person to person.
City lights would light the clouds and haze above a city, so the noon sky there would not be perfectly black.
Alpha Centauri never rises north of about 29 degrees north, so there the first star returns after 8.6 years (Sirius), and only in the season when Sirius is up at night.
Planets reflect sunlight and would be back within hours (Venus and Mars in minutes, Saturn in under three hours); the film does not show one.

claims.statement: The scenario removes all light for five seconds, including light in transit, then lets sources shine again.
With no light at all, people see a dark grey (eigengrau) produced by the visual system’s own noise rather than pure black.
claims.reasoning: Long-standing description of the intrinsic light of the eye.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Shown as a dark grey screen.

claims.statement: Light from a phone or lamp a few metres away arrives in nanoseconds, so nearby lights return instantly.
claims.reasoning: 10 m at 3e8 m/s is about 33 ns.

claims.statement: Sunlight takes about 499 seconds (8 minutes 19 seconds) to reach Earth, between about 490 and 507 s over the year.
claims.reasoning: 149.6 million km divided by the speed of light.

claims.statement: Until new sunlight arrives the daytime sky stays dark, because daylight is scattered sunlight and the light of the Moon, planets and stars in transit was erased too; only artificial lights shine.
claims.reasoning: Rayleigh scattering needs sunlight; reflected light from the Moon and planets is sunlight.

claims.statement: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight, so it returns with the Sun, about 1.3 seconds later.
claims.reasoning: Earth-Moon light time is about 1.28 s.

claims.statement: After the Sun, the nearest star is Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light-years away but far too faint to see; the nearest star you can see, Alpha Centauri A and B, is about 4.37 light-years (about 41 trillion km) away and only rises for viewers south of about 29 degrees north.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "The next closest is four years away, in the southern sky."

claims.statement: Sirius, 8.6 light-years away, is the nearest naked-eye star seen from mid-northern latitudes; the stars between 4.4 and 8.6 light-years (Barnard’s Star, Wolf 359, Lalande 21185) are too faint to see without a telescope. So up north the first star would return after about 8.6 years.
claims.reasoning: Each star returns after its light-travel time; magnitudes from the nearby-star tables.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Up north, your first star takes nearly nine years."

claims.statement: Light from the centre of the Sun’s disc arrives about 2.3 s before light from its edge (the Sun’s radius in light-seconds), so daylight would return over about two seconds rather than in one instant, most of it within the first second.
claims.reasoning: Solar radius 696,000 km divided by the speed of light; limb darkening weights the centre.

creative_direction.logline: At noon every light in the universe vanishes for five seconds: your phone comes back at once, the Sun takes eight minutes, and the stars take years.
creative_direction.visual_identity: A sunny street at eye level with an elegant boxless clock and countdowns in the top-left; eigengrau darkness; a lit city under a black noon sky; a light front crossing the orbits; a starless night; stars returning one by one.
creative_direction.lighting: Noon sun; then only lamps, signs, screens and headlights; then moonlight.
creative_direction.camera_language: Eye-level POV with your phone in frame; tilts up to the sky; a high orbital diagram; two locked-off sky time-lapses.
creative_direction.motion_language: Real-time darkness, then time-compressed waiting: a countdown in minutes, then in years.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Metre scale on the street; orbits to scale with enlarged bodies; true light-travel times.
creative_direction.opening_hook: Your phone goes black. So does the sun. For five seconds, there's no light anywhere.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: Your phone lights up after five seconds, but the noon sky stays black, because the new sunlight needs more than eight minutes to arrive.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: Five seconds of darkness: up north, the first star takes nearly nine years to come back.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The film opens on a clock in the top-left and ends on a year counter in the same place.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the city street, people, cars, sky rig and Moon; add a reusable distance-star-sky-v1 whose stars return by light-travel time.

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original score: a bright city pulse that cuts dead with the light, a held drone in the dark, a rising tone as sunlight races outward, a release chord when daylight returns, a wide quiet night, and a single chime for the first star.
audio.sfx_direction: Street ambience; a deep drop and gasps when light vanishes; braking cars; lights buzzing back; murmurs and idling engines under the black sky; silence before daylight; a chime for each returning star.

distribution.distinctive_angle: Five seconds without light is not five seconds of darkness: the Sun stays dark for eight minutes and the stars for years, because light takes time to travel.
distribution.comment_bait_question: Which star comes back first where you live?
distribution.seo_integrity_note: Light-travel times and star positions are real; the premise erases light in transit; the street is illustrative.
